gap: No result ChatGPT got states a named measurement for any kit priced between $3,000 and $4,000: the Anker SOLIX S5000 kit's own two PS400 panels peaked at 680 W of their 800 W rating and the station lost about 10 W on standby (Andrew Riha, pv magazine USA), while the Anker SOLIX F3800 delivered 2,905 Wh of its rated 3,840 Wh (Notebookcheck) against 3,790 Wh of 4,096 Wh for the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 (OutdoorGearLab).
standout_why: Compared against stormwatts.com (cited), lightsonlabs.com, preparedstates.com, powersized.com and Dealectric's own two ranking pages, all opened 2026-11-18. StormWatts, Lights On Labs and Prepared States each say they are spec-only and carry no reviewer measurement. PowerSized has two OutdoorGearLab capacity figures, but only for the BLUETTI AC180 and Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, both far below this budget. Dealectric's under-$3,000 page already has Notebookcheck drain tests for the Anker F3000, BLUETTI Elite 300 and Elite 400, so those are not new. None of the pages has a measurement for the S5000, F3800, DELTA Pro 3, Apex 300 or HomePower 3000, and none has a measured solar output for a kit's own panels in this price band. It is not a 3 because the figures come from different reviewers with different methods and the S5000 capacity figure is app-reported, not metered. solargenadvisor.com could not be opened (TLS certificate error), so it is not part of the comparison.
decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX S5000 + 2× 400 W kit ($3,599.99, ships now, a kit we link) as the pick. It is the only kit in the $3,000 to $4,000 band whose own panels have a named measured output (680 W peak), which makes the refill figure 7.4 h at measured peak against 6.3 h at rated output. Its app-reported 4.87 kWh delivered is the most of any candidate. Among the rival kits near $3,100, the measurements favour the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 over the Anker F3800 on energy delivered: 3,790 Wh against 2,905 to 2,980 Wh, although the F3800 is rated only 256 Wh smaller. The F3800 keeps its place only for a shopper who needs its 6,000 W output. For the BLUETTI Apex 300 + 2× 500 W pre-order, The Solar Lab's roughly 20 W idle draw is about twice the S5000's and 2.5 times the Jackery HomePower 3000's 8 W; that matters for a kit left on standby for outages.

findings.label: Measured solar output from two Anker PS400 panels (the panels in the 2× 400 W kit)
findings.value: 680 W peak, 85% of the 800 W combined rating
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review: 5 kWh on wheels, tested through a real power outage (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28; first published by ESS News 2026-10-25)
findings.note: Andrew Riha, pre-release unit, Northern California, sunny October day, two PS400 in series on the high-voltage input. Arithmetic: 5,024 Wh / 800 W = 6.3 h at rated output; 5,024 Wh / 680 W = 7.4 h at the measured peak. Both are best cases; a peak is not a day average and charging losses are not included.

findings.label: Energy delivered on a full discharge (app-reported, not metered)
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28)
findings.note: Riha writes that he did not meter the output; the figure is the Anker app's discharge reading, so it is not comparable one-to-one with the metered drain tests below. Arithmetic at the table's kit price: $3,599.99 / 4,870 Wh = $0.74 per app-reported delivered Wh.

findings.label: Wall energy for a full recharge and round-trip efficiency
findings.value: 6.24 kWh from the wall at the 1,800 W setting; 78% round trip
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28)
findings.note: Riha's calculation: 4.87 kWh out (app-reported) / 6.24 kWh in. Wall draw was about 1.79 kW for 2 h 49 min, then about 1.43 kW for the final 50 min, on 120 V.

findings.label: Standby loss with 120 V output on and nothing connected
findings.value: 5% state of charge in 24 hours, about 10 W
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28)
findings.note: Riha's measurement. Anker's own claim, quoted in the same review, is 8.8 W. Riha did not measure noise; the under-30 dB figure is Anker's.

findings.label: Runtime in a real outage
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28)
findings.note: PG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff; load was a large refrigerator plus phones and small devices. Arithmetic: 82% of 5,024 Wh = about 4,120 Wh over 61.5 h, about 67 W average.

findings.label: Measured energy output against rated capacity
findings.source_title: EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 Review (OutdoorGearLab, Kenji Mowrey, 2026-01-13)
findings.note: Measured on OutdoorGearLab's test jig; load not stated. OutdoorGearLab lists usable capacity as 93%; 3,790 / 4,096 works out to 92.5%. It also measured a 114.1 lb weight, a peak of about 1,600 W on a 15 A outlet (rated 1,800 W) and an average charging speed of 1,293 Wh/hr. No noise or solar figure was measured.

findings.label: Drain test, energy delivered
findings.value: 2,905 Wh of 3,840 Wh, about 75%, at a constant draw of about 260 W
findings.source_title: Anker Solix F3800 hands-on review (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten, 2024-08-27)
findings.note: Ran about 11 hours until shut-off at 1%. A full charge from 1% to 100% required 4,669 Wh from the wall, so about 62% of the AC energy was reusable (Schwarten's figure). AC charge took about 1 h 45 min with a measured peak of 2,966 W.

findings.label: Second drain test, energy delivered before inverter cut-off
findings.value: 2,980 Wh of 3,840 Wh; 4,930 Wh from the wall to charge 0 to 100%
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800: Do We Really Need Gas Generators? (StorageReview, Kevin OBrien, 2024-06-21)
findings.note: Load profile not stated. Arithmetic: 2,980 / 3,840 = 77.6% of rated; 2,980 / 4,930 = 60% round trip. StorageReview also measured UPS switchover at 13 ms to battery and 14 ms back (maker's rating 20 ms). The two reviewers agree within 75 Wh.

findings.label: Noise under heavy load
findings.value: about 42 dB at 1 m while delivering 3,000 W
findings.source_title: Anker Solix F3800 hands-on review (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten, 2024-08-27)
findings.note: Same reviewer and distance as the F3000 figure below, so the two are comparable.

findings.label: Drain tests at two loads, and noise
findings.value: about 2,500 Wh of 3,072 Wh (81%) at about 200 W; almost 2,800 Wh (91%) at 1,800 W; about 35 dB at 1 m at about 3,000 W
findings.source_title: Powerhouse with 3.6 kW and 3 kWh: Anker Solix F3000 review (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten, 2026-02-20)
findings.note: The 200 W figure is already on Dealectric's under-$3,000 page; the 1,800 W result and the noise figure are not. A full charge used 3,480 Wh from the wall in 1 h 20 min. Solar could not be tested at full power (winter, Hamburg). Against the F3800 by the same reviewer: the F3000 is 7 dB quieter at about 3,000 W and delivers nearly as much energy at high load as the F3800 did at 260 W.

findings.label: Efficiency and idle draw
findings.value: about 85% efficiency across a variety of AC loads; idle draw about 20 W
findings.source_title: Bluetti Apex 300 review (The Solar Lab; no author or date on the page, footer copyright 2026)
findings.note: The Solar Lab does not report Wh delivered or per-load results, or whether AC output was on for the idle figure. Arithmetic: 2,764.8 Wh / 20 W = about 138 h, which matches the page's 'about 6 days'. Applies to the Apex 300 + 2× 500 W kit ($3,134.05 link price, pre-order with dispatch late January 2027).

findings.label: Idle consumption
findings.source_title: Jackery HomePower 3000 Review: Is Jackery's First HomePower Unit a Good Purchase? (The Solar Lab; no author or date on the page, footer copyright 2026)
findings.note: Same reviewer as the Apex 300 idle figure, so the two are comparable: 8 W against about 20 W. Arithmetic: 3,072 Wh / 8 W = 384 h, about 16 days; the page says 'over two weeks'. The page gives no efficiency, delivered-Wh, noise or solar measurement.

findings.label: Drain tests (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten), as already printed on Dealectric's under-$3,000 page
findings.value: Elite 400: about 3,130 Wh of 3,840 Wh (just under 82%) at about 250 W; Elite 300: about 2,650 Wh of 3,014.4 Wh (just under 88%) at just over 200 W

findings.note: I read these on our own page, not on Notebookcheck, in this run; reopen the Notebookcheck reviews before reprinting. Listed so the side-by-side table is complete. Not new against the ChatGPT results, since our page is result 2.

findings.label: Measured output of the 200 W panels that ship in rival and BLUETTI kits (OutdoorGearLab), as already printed on Dealectric's panels-included page
findings.value: Jackery SolarSaga 200: 171 W; Anker SOLIX PS200: 166 W; Bluetti 200 W portable: 150 W

findings.note: I read these on our own page, not on OutdoorGearLab, in this run; reopen the OutdoorGearLab panel reviews before reprinting. Arithmetic for 2× 200 W kits: Jackery 342 W, BLUETTI 300 W. None of these is the 400 W or 500 W panel in the kits above $3,000.

findings.label: What the rival pages hold on measurements
findings.value: StormWatts, Lights On Labs and Prepared States: no reviewer measurements, each states it is spec-only; PowerSized: two OutdoorGearLab capacity figures (BLUETTI AC180 950 Wh, Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 1,710 Wh), none for a kit above $1,700
findings.source_title: Solar Generator Kits Compared at the Same Panel Watts: Jackery vs EcoFlow vs Anker vs BLUETTI | StormWatts
findings.note: Also opened 2026-11-18: https://www.lightsonlabs.com/power-stations/best-solar-generators/ , https://www.preparedstates.com/kit/solar-generators , https://powersized.com/best/solar-generator/ . StormWatts has one owner-run day (800 W of SolarSaga 200 W panels on a Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus peaking at 696 W on October 29), which is not one of the kits in this budget band.

unsourced: solargenadvisor.com/best-solar-generator-kits/ (result 10): the page would not open (TLS certificate error), so I could not check it for measurements.

A metered (not app-reported) drain test of the Anker SOLIX S5000, and a measured noise figure for it: Riha's review has neither, and I found no Notebookcheck, OutdoorGearLab or StorageReview test of the S5000.

A metered drain test of the BLUETTI Apex 300: Notebookcheck's review (Christian Hintze, 2025-08-10, opened) reports no drain test, standby or dB figure; an Outdoor Life figure of 2,290 Wh (83%) and a Digital Trends DELTA Pro 3 figure of 3.7 kWh appeared only in search snippets and I did not open those pages, so they are left out.
Any named measurement for the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus: one search returned only retailer and spec pages.
A delivered-Wh drain test for the Jackery HomePower 3000: I found only The Solar Lab's idle figure.
Any named measurement for the ALLPOWERS R3500: not searched in this run; our under-$3,000 page says none was found.
Any named measurement for the BLUETTI 5kWh RV Kit: not searched in this run.

Measured output of the other kit panels in this band (BLUETTI 500 W, EcoFlow 400 W, Anker 400 W bifacial sold with the F3000 and F3800): the F3000 and Apex 300 reviewers both said the weather prevented a full solar test.
Measured noise and idle draw for the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: OutdoorGearLab gives no dB or standby figure.

Today's bundle prices for the rival kits (DELTA Pro 3 + 400 W, F3800 + 400 W, HomePower 3600 Plus + 2× 200 W): this angle did not open the store pages, so the $3,099 figures are only what ChatGPT's cards and Lights On Labs (2026-10-27) showed, and I did no per-delivered-Wh arithmetic on them.
